key_facts: **Lichen planus** is a T-cell–mediated inflammatory disease of skin, mucosa, hair and nails.
The **6 Ps**: purple, polygonal, planar, pruritic papules and plaques, with white **Wickham striae**; flexor wrists, lower back, ankles.
Check the **mouth**, genitals, nails and scalp; oral LP is often lace-like and white.
Ask about drugs (lichenoid drug eruption) and consider **hepatitis C** testing according to risk.
Potent topical steroids for skin; refer mucosal, nail, scalp (scarring) or extensive disease.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Lichen planus (LP)** is an idiopathic inflammatory disorder of skin and/or mucosa presenting with intensely itchy **flat-topped, violaceous, polygonal papules**. Classic cutaneous LP favours **flexor wrists**, lumbar back, ankles. Mucosal, nail, scalp (lichen planopilaris), and genital variants exist. Association with **hepatitis C** is described in some populations — screen selectively by risk/prevalence.

sub: Adults 30–60; cutaneous LP affects about 1% of people, oral LP 1–2%.
Skin LP usually clears within 1–2 years; oral and genital LP are often chronic.

ul: T-cell mediated attack on basal keratinocytes (lichenoid interface dermatitis).

Triggers: idiopathic; drugs (**lichenoid drug eruption** — e.g. some antihypertensives, antimalarials, gold, TNF inhibitors — take drug history); dental amalgam sometimes linked to oral LP; HCV association variable by region.
Koebnerisation along scratch lines possible.
Autoimmune attack on basal keratinocytes, possibly triggered by altered self-antigens (viral, drug).
Drugs: beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, thiazides, antimalarials, gold, checkpoint inhibitors.
**"LP is contagious"**: it is not.
**"Oral LP is just a mouth ulcer"**: chronic erosive oral LP carries a small risk of SCC and needs follow-up.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Cytotoxic T cells attack the **basal layer** of the epidermis (an **interface dermatitis**).

mech.t: An altered antigen on basal keratinocytes is presented to T cells.
CD8+ T cells form a dense **band** along the dermo-epidermal junction and kill basal cells (apoptotic **Civatte bodies**).
mech.caption: Flat-topped violaceous polygonal papules with Wickham striae and a Koebner line.

mech.t: The epidermis responds with a thick granular layer and **saw-tooth** rete ridges: seen clinically as Wickham striae.
Melanin falls into the dermis (pigment incontinence), causing long-lasting **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation**, especially in darker skin.
In the mouth the same process causes white reticular lace and painful erosions.
mech.caption: Reticular oral lichen planus on the buccal mucosa.

histo: Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction, hypergranulosis, saw-tooth acanthosis, Civatte bodies; direct immunofluorescence shows fibrinogen along the basement membrane.

Full exam: skin, mouth, nails, scalp, genitals.
**Punch biopsy** if uncertain (band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, saw-tooth acanthosis, civatte bodies).
Consider HCV testing based on risk/local guidance; drug review for lichenoid drug eruption.

ladder.t: Emollients; avoid vigorous scrubbing of the scale.
**Potent / very potent topical steroid ointment** to itchy papules, short courses (caution thin skin). Antihistamine for itch (sedating at night).
Stop the culprit drug with its prescriber if lichenoid drug eruption suspected.
Oral, genital, nail, extensive or scalp disease → dermatology / oral medicine: steroid mouth preparations, systemic steroids, phototherapy, immunosuppressants.

refer.t: Non-healing oral ulcer, thickening white patch or lump in long-standing oral LP: **refer urgently** (oral SCC).
Genital erosions, scarring or dyspareunia: refer (vulval / penile LP).
Scalp redness with scarring hair loss: early referral (lichen planopilaris).

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Non-healing oral ulcer, white patch that thickens or a lump in long-standing oral LP: **refer urgently** (oral SCC).
Genital erosions, scarring or dyspareunia: refer (vulval or penile LP).
Scalp redness with scarring hair loss: lichen planopilaris, early referral.
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
Scarring alopecia and permanent nail loss.
Vulval/penile scarring; small risk of SCC in chronic erosive oral or genital LP.
Cutaneous LP: most resolves in 1–2 years; hypertrophic LP persists longer. Mucosal LP is often lifelong.

pearls: Warn about post-inflammatory pigment lasting months.
Advise against vigorous scrubbing of Wickham-striae scale.
Sexual health / genital itch: examine and refer early if erosive.
Document HCV risk discussion where relevant.
